segments.narration: One woman's DNA turned up at forty crime scenes. She was tied to burglaries, car thefts and six killings across three countries over sixteen years.
Germany built a task force for her and raised the reward to 300,000 euros. No witness ever described her. No camera ever caught her.
Her profile sat beside a murdered police officer in Heilbronn, and beside petty break-ins hundreds of miles away. What criminal leaves DNA and nothing else?
In March 2009, investigators finally tested the swabs themselves. The DNA was already on them, before anyone touched a single crime scene.
It belonged to a woman at the factory that packed them. The hunt ended, and in 2016 the ISO published a standard for DNA-free swabs.

verdicts.claim: Between 1993 and 2009 the same unidentified female DNA profile was recovered from about 40 crime scenes in Germany, Austria and France, six of them murders.

verdicts.claim: The profile was recovered at the scene of the killing of police officer Michele Kiesewetter in Heilbronn on 25 April 2007 as well as at minor property crimes far away.

verdicts.claim: In March 2009 investigators concluded the DNA had already been present on the cotton swabs before they were used to collect samples, so no such offender existed.

verdicts.claim: The DNA belonged to a woman working at the factory that made the swabs, and the case led the International Organization for Standardization to publish ISO 18385 in 2016 for DNA-free forensic consumables.

candidates.why: A single number that immediately implies an impossible person.

candidates.text: Europe's most wanted criminal did not actually exist
candidates.why: Strong line but it gives away the ending in the first sentence.

candidates.text: Police offered three hundred thousand euros for a ghost
candidates.why: The reward figure plus 'ghost'; evocative, but vaguer about what actually happened.

choice.reason: It creates the mystery instead of spoiling it, and forty scenes is concrete enough to feel impossible on the first listen.
